opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so in the earlier rounds, 2016 and 2022, we only surveyed people who'd published at NeurIPS and ICML. Those are the two big flagship machine learning conferences, so it was a reasonable starting point. But there was a fair criticism that this is a fairly particular slice of the field. It's heavily deep-learning-flavored, and you might worry you're getting a population that's more bullish, or just more homogeneous in outlook, than AI researchers broadly.

So for the 2023 survey we wanted to widen it out, and the question was roughly: what are the top-tier venues where serious AI research gets published, such that a reasonable person would say "yes, these are AI researchers"? We ended up adding ICLR, which is arguably now in the same tier as NeurIPS and ICML for machine learning, plus AAAI and IJCAI, which are older, more general AI conferences and bring in people from more traditional AI areas like planning, knowledge representation, and search. We also added JMLR, the main journal in the area, partly because some people publish primarily in journals.

The guiding idea was to stay fairly selective. We didn't want to dilute things by including every workshop or niche venue, where it gets harder to say who counts as an expert. But we wanted enough breadth that if someone said "you only asked the deep learning crowd," we'd have a good answer. That also let us check whether answers differed by venue. My recollection is that the differences weren't dramatic, which was somewhat reassuring about the earlier results.

It also roughly doubled our sample, to a couple of thousand respondents, I think, which helps with all the subgroup analysis and the noisier questions.

r001.rationale: The response says AAAI and IJCAI bring in researchers from traditional AI areas such as planning, knowledge representation, and search, broadening the survey beyond the deep-learning-heavy crowd.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that the original choice of NeurIPS and ICML wasn't really ours in any deep sense. When we did the 2016 survey, we just wanted the people who were doing the kind of machine learning work that seemed most relevant to where AI was heading, and those two were the obvious top venues for that. So in 2022, when we wanted to broaden it, the question was really, what does that same intention look like now that the field is much bigger and more fragmented?

Our concern was that if you only survey NeurIPS and ICML, you're getting a particular slice. You're getting a lot of the deep learning mainstream, but you're maybe underrepresenting people in natural language processing, or computer vision, or more theoretical corners, who are still clearly AI researchers and might have different views. And we didn't want our results to be an artifact of two conferences' particular cultures.

So we looked at the venues people generally treat as top tier in the subfields, things like ACL and EMNLP for language, CVPR and ICCV for vision, ICLR, AAAI, IJCAI, JMLR, and so on. We ended up with six venues, and the main criterion was honestly fairly pragmatic: well regarded, large enough to give us a real sample, and with authorship that we could actually track down and email. That last part matters more than you'd think. A lot of the work is just getting contact information, so a venue where authors are reachable is worth a lot.

And then one thing we did care about was being able to compare with the earlier surveys, so we kept NeurIPS and ICML in there and we report breakdowns by venue. We were curious whether the broader set would move the headline numbers, and it turned out the picture was pretty similar across venues, which was somewhat reassuring. It suggested the views weren't just a NeurIPS phenomenon. Though I'd still say, that's a sample of people who publish at top venues, and I wouldn't want anyone to read it as representing everyone who works on AI.

r001.rationale: The response says relying only on NeurIPS and ICML would underrepresent researchers in areas such as NLP, computer vision, and theory, even though they are AI researchers, and gives that as a reason to broaden the survey.

astra-6.text: We wanted to get a broader cross-section of AI research, rather than just people publishing at NeurIPS and ICML. So the idea was to include prominent venues covering different areas of AI, while keeping the sampling process reasonably systematic. There’s a trade-off there: you want broader coverage, but you also need a manageable set of venues and a consistent way to identify the researchers you’re going to invite.

r001.rationale: The response says it sought broader coverage across AI research areas, but does not clearly identify including researchers outside machine learning as a reason.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted to get a broader sample of AI researchers, rather than just people publishing at NeurIPS and ICML. So we included other major machine learning venues, as well as more general AI venues. There’s a trade-off between covering the field broadly and having a reasonably clear, practical way to identify researchers to contact. Publication at those venues gave us a consistent sampling criterion, though it certainly doesn’t capture everyone working on AI.

r001.rationale: The response says they added more general AI venues alongside machine learning venues to get a broader sample, communicating inclusion of researchers outside machine learning.
